analysis.one_liner: Stops three interstate river basin commissions from regulating fracking unless states themselves set the rules.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Rep. Scott Perry with 6 Republican cosponsors, was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The DRILL Now Act would amend the Water Resources Development Act of 2007 to bar the Susquehanna, Delaware, and Potomac River Basin Commissions from finalizing, implementing, or enforcing any rule on hydraulic fracturing unless the rule was issued by the state itself. Because these multi-state commissions can adopt basin-wide rules that bind all member states, the bill would strip them of the power to restrict fracking across the basins, leaving only state-by-state rules in place. The bill was referred to committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Natural gas drilling companies and landowners with mineral rights in the Susquehanna, Delaware, and Potomac river basins. The bill would remove the possibility of basin-wide fracking restrictions from the interstate commissions, opening more of the Delaware River Basin — where a multi-state fracking ban was adopted in 2021 — to drilling under Pennsylvania's state rules alone. Supporters framed it as protecting landowners' ability to develop their property and as a response to energy price pressure in early 2022.

how_it_helps.text: The bill bars the Susquehanna River Basin Commission, the Delaware River Basin Commission, and the Interstate Commission on the Potomac River Basin from finalizing, implementing, or enforcing any regulation relating to hydraulic fracturing unless it was issued by the state where it would apply.
It does this by amending Section 5019 of the Water Resources Development Act of 2007, overriding the fracking-related authority of the interstate compacts that created the three commissions.

The bill's stated purpose, reflected in its title, is to stop what it calls regulatory interference with landowners and legislatures — preserving landowners' ability to develop their mineral rights and leaving fracking policy to each state's legislature and regulators.

analysis.who_pays: Residents of the three river basins — the Delaware basin alone supplies drinking water to roughly 13 million people — who would lose the layer of multi-state water protection the commissions provide. The basin commissions themselves would lose authority over fracking, and states that voted against basin-wide fracking rules through the commissions (such as New York, New Jersey, and Delaware in the Delaware basin) would be bound only by the rules of whatever state hosts the drilling site.

drawbacks.text: The bill would strip the multi-state Delaware River Basin Commission of its authority to restrict fracking, effectively undoing the basin-wide fracking ban its member states adopted in 2021 and exposing the drinking-water source for millions of people to drilling activity under Pennsylvania's state rules alone.
It overrides interstate compacts that Congress itself ratified into law, weakening the long-established structure by which member states jointly manage shared water resources.
An honest supporter must acknowledge that multi-state basins cross state lines, so state-by-state rules alone leave downstream states with no say over pollution generated upstream of them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit — faster permitting and more drilling access for gas producers and mineral-rights owners — is concentrated and specific. The cost is diffuse but large: weakened protections for the drinking-water supply of millions of people in three shared river basins, and a rollback of the multi-state governance structure those states built for their shared waters. On balance, the bill's design serves the drilling industry far more than the general public.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to its Water Resources and Environment subcommittee, and it sat there with no further action until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Scott Perry introduced the DRILL Now Act in the House on February 8, 2022, with 6 Republican cosponsors.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.

The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment, and the action history shows no further steps — no markup, no committee report, no floor vote — before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The bill died quietly, so basin residents and the states that backed basin-wide fracking restrictions are better off than they would have been if it had passed. Gas drilling companies face no change; their interests are preserved by inaction.

for.name: Rep. Scott Perry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to strip the three river basin commissions of fracking regulatory authority.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of referral; never scheduled a markup
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 8, 2022 and never reported the bill out; the action history shows the bill went no further than a subcommittee referral.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 6 cosponsors were Republicans, and no Democrat signed on; the bill died in a committee controlled by the Democratic majority without any recorded votes.

industries.note: The bill would remove basin-wide fracking restrictions from the three river basin commissions, opening more acreage — including parts of the Delaware Basin under its 2021 fracking ban — to drilling under state rules alone. That gain comes directly at the expense of multi-state drinking-water protections for basin residents.

industries.industry: Landowners with mineral rights in the Susquehanna, Delaware, and Potomac basins
industries.note: The bill's title frames it as protecting landowners from interstate commissions restricting development of their mineral property. This is a genuine gain for those owners, though it is a narrow and concentrated group rather than the general public.

The bill directly strips the Susquehanna, Delaware, and Potomac Basin Commissions of any fracking regulatory role, hollowing out the multi-state water-management structure Congress created. Their loss of authority removes a protection for the public's shared water resources.
